lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What is a closure in JavaScript?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the place where it was created.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It keeps them even after the outer function has finished. Let us build one.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The function [makeCounter|make counter] creates a variable called count.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It returns an inner function that changes count, and returns it.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: When [makeCounter|make counter] finishes, you would expect count to disappear.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: But the inner function still holds a reference to it. That is the closure.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Call it once and you get one. Call it again and you get two.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Each call to [makeCounter|make counter] creates a new closure, with its own count.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And the outside cannot reach count at all. It is private.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What about the famous loop question?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: With [var|var], all three callbacks share one variable. When the timers fire, i is already three.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: With [let|let], every iteration gets its own copy, so you get zero, one, two.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Where would I use this in real code?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Function factories. [makeAdder|make adder] remembers the number you gave it.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Add five to three is eight. Add ten to three is thirteen. Each function remembers its own number.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Closures give you private state, function factories, and callbacks that remember their context.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So a closure is a function, plus the scope it remembers.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Exactly. That is your interview answer.
